patient.chief_complaint: Sudden right-sided weakness and sensory loss — 48 hours
patient.history_present_illness: Ms. W is a 29-year-old nursing student with established quiescent SLE who presents with 48 hours of right-sided arm and leg weakness and right hemisensory loss. She has had SLE for 4 years, managed with hydroxychloroquine, with no prior major organ involvement and quiescent disease activity for 18 months. Her rheumatologist last assessed her 3 months ago with normal complement levels and stable anti-dsDNA. The neurological symptoms began abruptly 48 hours ago without any prodrome. She has been in good health and her SLE has been well-controlled. She failed a clinical rotation assessment 3 weeks ago and is concerned about dismissal from her nursing program. Her nursing training makes her familiar with lupus cerebritis, antiphospholipid syndrome, and CNS vasculitis, and she is worried about CNS lupus involvement. She has no prior neurological presentations. She has no fever, no joint pain flare, no rash, and no renal symptoms. She denies headache. On directed questioning, she acknowledges significant stress from the nursing program failure and feels her symptoms began after a particularly difficult study session. The diagnostic challenge is distinguishing FND from neuropsychiatric SLE, which is a real entity in SLE patients with cerebrovascular, inflammatory, or autoantibody-mediated mechanisms.

output.query: neuropsychiatric lupus NPSLE diagnosis criteria attribution

results.title: 2019 European League Against Rheumatism recommendations for management of NPSLE

output.summary: EULAR 2019 recommendations for NPSLE: attribution to SLE requires positive biomarkers (elevated anti-dsDNA, low complement, CSF pleocytosis or elevated protein, neuroimaging evidence) AND exclusion of other causes. In this case: quiescent SLE serology (normal complement, negative anti-dsDNA, SLEDAI 0), negative APS serology, normal MRI, normal CSF, and positive functional signs — all criteria favor FND attribution rather than NPSLE.

output.proposed: No new medications — reviewing current regimen
interactions: Hydroxychloroquine + sertraline: both QTc-prolonging agents. Combination can prolong QTc — baseline ECG recommended. At current doses, risk is generally low.
No pharmacokinetic interaction between hydroxychloroquine and sertraline
warnings: ECG recommended to assess baseline QTc given hydroxychloroquine + sertraline combination

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Functional neurological disorder — right-sided functional hemimotor syndrome, in patient with quiescent SLE (neuropsychiatric SLE excluded)

differential.key_feature: Quiescent SLE serology (complement normal, anti-dsDNA negative, SLEDAI 0), negative APS serology (triple negative aCL/LAC/anti-beta2GPI), normal MRI without infarcts or white matter disease, normal CSF — all EULAR attribution criteria favor against NPSLE
Triple-negative APS serology (aCL, lupus anticoagulant, anti-beta2GPI all negative) definitively excludes APS; MRI DWI negative
No MRI enhancement or infarct pattern of vasculitis; normal CSF without pleocytosis; quiescent disease activity
MRI DWI negative; age 29 with no traditional vascular risk factors; antiphospholipid syndrome excluded

optimal_actions.expected_finding: Normal — no infarct, no CNS lupus white matter disease

optimal_actions.expected_finding: Normal — no focal slowing or epileptiform activity

critical_actions: APS triple panel — must exclude antiphospholipid syndrome stroke in SLE patient
Rheumatology consultation for SLE activity assessment
contraindicated_actions: High-dose corticosteroids or cyclophosphamide without confirmed active NPSLE — quiescent disease does not require escalation
Ignoring SLE history and jumping to FND without rigorous NPSLE exclusion
key_reasoning_points: SLE patients with neurological symptoms require rigorous exclusion of NPSLE before FND diagnosis — EULAR criteria require positive biomarkers AND neuroimaging evidence for NPSLE attribution
Triple-negative APS serology (aCL, lupus anticoagulant, anti-beta2GPI) definitively excludes antiphospholipid syndrome — this is the most common cause of stroke in young SLE patients
Quiescent SLE (complement normal, anti-dsDNA negative, SLEDAI 0) makes acute CNS lupus flare very unlikely
After rigorous organic exclusion, positive functional signs (Hoover, distractibility) confirm FND as the diagnosis

red_herrings.data_point: Known SLE diagnosis in a young Black female
red_herrings.intended_effect: Attribute all neurological symptoms to NPSLE without checking activity biomarkers
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: SLE is quiescent with normal complement, negative anti-dsDNA, and SLEDAI 0; APS triple-negative; normal CSF and MRI — NPSLE attribution criteria not met; FND with identified psychological precipitant is the correct diagnosis

metadata.notes: Moderate FND — right hemimotor in quiescent SLE patient. Must exclude NPSLE and APS rigorously before FND diagnosis. APS triple panel critical.
